items.title: Land is the Leader
items.summary: Kukui and Gary Maunakea created a farm for young people inspired by by aloha ʻāina, which is the love of land, or the love of the land which feeds us. Farming 250, A Series with Civil Eats focuses on the question is being asked: What does America look like right now? In this new series, Farming 250, Civil Eats seeks to answer that question from the soil up. The newsroom is partnering with NPQ for the #WeTheCivic America 250 campaign. We thought that we’d start an organization that would provide a challenge for young people, a challenge for them to work to solve a problem in the community, and at the same time we would help support them through college, but then also employ them on the farm. Young people were pivotal from the very first iteration of MA‘O Organic Farms. We were inspired by the work of pre-contact Hawaiians, who actually grew 100 percent of their food: both the structure, the engineered systems to grow food, and the values and practices they had to back that up. We’ve realized that they’re willing to take up this kuleana, this responsibility, but only on certain terms. Like they don’t want to farm one product—that would just chase them away. They want to farm with other young people. We really believed in the goal of mentoring young people, but not forgetting that there is peer-to-peer mentoring that’s possible.

items.title: ‘Get your hands in the soil, leave with fresh produce’
items.summary: Stephanie Gomez, a farmer in San Fernando Valley remembers what communal gardening looked like from her grandfather. For her, access to green space and farmers is how we can build a successful food system. Farming 250, A Series with Civil Eats, focuses on the question is being asked: What does America look like right now? In this new series, Farming 250, Civil Eats seeks to answer that question from the soil up. The newsroom is partnering with NPQ for the #WeTheCivic America 250 campaign. I had a grandfather who was a jardinero, so he would maintain people’s gardens. Sometimes I would go to work with him and watch him do his work, hold his tools. In his own home he grew like five different orange trees, he had an apple tree, he always had a variety of chiles. He even had a section with nopales, with chicken wire around it so we wouldn’t fall into it. This was here in Los Angeles, in Highland Park. And then my other grandpa lived closer to East LA. He had an apartment, but in the complex they had a communal area, and in that communal area they had a lime tree, and my grandpa would care for chickens that lived under the tree. I remember going out there and having to feed them, and running away from them because I didn’t want to get pecked. I remember early on what it meant for me to have culturally rich foods—Mexican cuisine that was so delicious and memorable.

items.title: What’s happening with Section 504—and how are nonprofits fighting?
items.summary: Federal disability-rights laws remain in place, but advocates say the loss of key HHS regulations creates uncertainty around community integration. Nonprofits are mobilizing. On September 23, 2026, a federal court removed six provisions from the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) regulations that spelled out how federally funded programs are supposed to protect community-integration rights: the rights of people with disabilities to live, work, and receive public support in the most community-integrated setting possible. This was the Texas v. Kennedy order—and it applies nationally across the United States. Federal disability law still protects community integration, and those protections reach far beyond people with physical disabilities, intellectual or developmental disabilities, or autism. More than 8.4 million Medicaid beneficiaries received home- and community-based services (HCBS) in 2023. Those services included home health, personal care, rehabilitative services, waiver programs, and other supports that allowed people—including older adults—to receive help outside institutional settings. The Medicaid count doesn’t even capture everyone whose community-integration rights may be at stake. Amber Smock, vice president of advocacy at Access Living in Chicago, Illinois, stressed that community integration also impacts nonprofit systems serving people with mental health disabilities, people in substance-use recovery, and disabled people experiencing homelessness. Permanent supportive housing, she explained, can combine housing with services to help someone remain in the community rather than go into an institution.

items.title: We Can Become Stronger Together
items.summary: Tiffany St. Goddard, a farmer and rancher speaks to the power and importance of gathering community in spaces such as Spirit of the Horse, a one-day, leadership-through-horsemanship camp for Blackfeet girls and the Rooted in the Land program—created by Indigenous women, for Indigenous women. Farming 250, A Series with Civil Eats focuses on the question is being asked: What does America look like right now? In this new series, Farming 250, Civil Eats seeks to answer that question from the soil up. The newroom is partnering with NPQ for the #WeTheCivic America 250 campaign. I have always grown up around horses. My whole life, I’ve been just a crazy little horse girl. I used to go outside and bring cereal treats to a horse of mine. He was a young horse, so we basically grew up together. I just knew I always wanted to be around horses. My parents, my family and I are all enrolled members of the Blackfeet Tribe. My dad is a big outdoorsman, more the hunting, packing type. On my mom’s side, my grandpa and mom raised cattle, so I grew up around that, around brandings, around cows. I just knew I always wanted horses in my life. I also enjoyed cattle, and then when I got with my husband, back in our college days, his family was big into cattle, and so it just kind of naturally flowed I guess you could say. Right now, we own and raise registered quarter horses. We train horses and sell them. My husband and I also do colt starting and training, so we have some client horses that we take in. We like to get them to a good place in their life, to where they’re going to do well and excel in the next person’s hands.

items.title: What happens when a fiscal sponsor shuts down?
items.summary: The closure of the High Desert Community Foundation fiscal sponsorship program forces nonprofits to consider what happens when community projects depend on a shared nonprofit structure—and when that structure gets taken away. The High Desert Community Foundation (HDCF) has announced it will end its fiscal sponsorship program on December 31, 2026, with operations expected to cease by the end of June 2027. This means the foundation’s sponsored projects will need to establish their own independent nonprofit status or find another fiscal sponsor. HDCF’s decision, announced on July 30, affects more than just the foundation itself. The foundation had previously stated that its sponsorship program supports more than 30 community projects in youth development, healthcare access, food insecurity, and services for underserved communities. HDCF provides the projects with the financial, legal, and organizational structure needed that allows them to operate. The closure of the funding program forces nonprofits and community project leaders to consider what happens when multiple community projects depend on a shared nonprofit structure, and what happens when that structure gets taken away. Creating a nonprofit involves substantial paperwork and ongoing compliance, plus it takes time and money. Fiscal sponsorships allow a project to operate through an existing nonprofit organization rather than having the project create its own tax-exempt status. Fiscal sponsorships can provide the legal and financial infrastructure behind a project, such as managing funds, receiving charitable contributions, handling the accounting, and providing compliance support.

items.title: Who fills the gap when philanthropy walks away from social justice movements?
items.summary: A call to organize when several major funders have significantly cut their funding to support social justice movements. Philanthropy has spent generations positioning itself as a foundational pillar of civil rights and social justice work in this country. So, why aren’t we treating these exits as a betrayal of the very role philanthropy has defined for itself? And, most importantly, what are we doing as a sector to chart a new path forward to sustain our collective efforts to advance social justice? In the past three months, multiple foundations have announced previously unplanned moves to wind down their funding allocations on multiple issues, such as immigration and LGBTQ+ rights. These funders have joined Wellspring Philanthropic Fund and several other institutions that have made the same decision in the past two years. For example, just a few months ago—without a major announcement—Foundation for a Just Society quietly made alarming cuts to its domestic social justice portfolio. In parallel, a number of reproductive health, rights, and justice funders have been swiftly and silently cutting back funding for movement-building reproductive justice organizations—even before Dobbs v. Jackson overturned the federal constitutional right to abortion. This has been happening in the backdrop of even more funders that significantly cut their funding for racial justice in recent years, with especially violent funding cuts for pro-Palestine organizations.

items.title: Women- and Indigenous-led community funds are rewriting the rules of US philanthropy
items.summary: For decades, women- and Indigenous-led institutions have designed their work around the belief that decisions about money should be made by, and with, the people those decisions affect. Large foundations still set the terms of American giving. Yet beside them, a quieter set of institutions has been working on another model for decades: women’s funds, giving circles, and funds led by Indigenous communities. They differ in size, budget and politics, but what they share is a belief that decisions about money should be made by, and with, the people those decisions affect. In Boston, for example, a grassroots organization can receive money from the Boston Women’s Fund without ever filling out a grant application. The fund does not send out a request for proposals for its Community Impact grants. Instead, the public nominates groups, and an allocations committee made up of community members interviews the leaders and the people they serve. The fund’s 2023 grants followed what it calls “Requests for Conversations,” which replaced written applications so that grassroots leaders could keep their time for their own organizations. It is a small detail, but it shows what happens when the people closest to a problem help control the purse. The questions philanthropy usually answers from the top—namely who is trusted, who carries the risk, and who makes decisions—get answered differently.

items.title: Beyond November: Democracy needs philanthropy to think past the next election
items.summary: Funders focused on the 2026 election may miss a critical point: Sustaining our democracy will require funding that goes beyond a single election cycle. The midterm election presents another perilous moment for our democracy, and funders have mobilized to help. Faced with a federal administration determined to limit voting and erode the rule of law, American philanthropy has rallied to support voters and the state officials working to keep the midterm elections free, fair, and secure. One-time, short-term grants, even robust ones, won’t provide a counter to the anti-democracy movement that is very much in place for the long haul. But funders who are understandably focused on the 2026 election, especially those who have recently expanded their portfolios to add democracy protection, may miss a critical point: Sustaining our democracy will require funding that goes beyond a single election cycle. Threats to the midterm election represent a crisis, to be sure. But simply surviving the crisis of the moment is not enough. The efforts of President Trump and his allies to push conspiracy theories and undermine election integrity will not stop after November—or even after Trump’s term. The president is exploiting all the federal power he can while in office, but he and his supporters have built a movement that will outlast him. Election deniers hold public office, legions of allies have organized at the grassroots level, and there is an entire media apparatus dedicated to confusing and frightening voters.

items.title: From Boxes to Watercolors: Rethinking Data and Belonging for Multiracial People
items.summary: The nonprofit sector's culture and language is built upon the assumption that each person belongs to exactly one racial group. Yet Multiracial people practice a form of bridging that movement-building and coalition work genuinely need. When I was five days old, my father filled out my birth certificate paperwork at a clinic in Brussels, Belgium. When he wrote my name, he was told he needed special permission to use that name for me. After several visits to the vital records office and an official letter from the Indian embassy, the clinic finally agreed to enter my name. I was a newborn but already too complicated for the form. I am Indian and White American, and for as long as I can remember, official forms have had a place to put half of me but nowhere my whole self. I’m not alone in this: 34 million people in the US now identify as Multiracial, a population that grew by 276 percent between 2010 and 2020. Some of that growth is people finally being able to claim all of who they are on a form. You would not know any of this from looking at the nonprofit and philanthropic sector’s own infrastructure. Our data systems, our everyday language, and the assumptions baked into how we organize solidarity are all built around the idea that everyone fits into exactly one box. Even some of the most progressive organizations fighting every day for racial justice do not “see” or account for the Multiracial experience.

items.title: Voting While Indigenous: 3 Perspectives on the Role of Voting in Our Ongoing Battle for Liberation
items.summary: NDN Collective is committed to the liberation of Indigenous Peoples, which requires a multifaceted approach to organizing political power. Relatives, we know that voting as an Indigenous person can be complicated. Long distances to polling stations, no guaranteed time off work to vote, confusing requirements for mailing addresses, and shifting ID laws work to intentionally suppress the votes of marginalized people (we plan to dive deeper into these systemic issues another time). As we gear up for the midterm elections in November, we think it’s important to begin discussing what Choctaw journalist B. ‘Toastie’ Oaster called the “Native Vote Dilemma” – that existential question of how we engage with the political system that colonized our land and continues functioning as a settler-colonial nation-state. At NDN Collective, we are committed to the liberation of Indigenous Peoples – which requires a multi-faceted approach to organized political power. “We must understand the politics of our community, and we must know what politics is supposed to produce. We must know what politics play in our lives.” The nuances around voting as Indigenous people cannot be summed up in a simple slogan. So instead, we are leaning into the complexities and contradictions of voting while Indigenous. We spoke with three colleagues at NDN Collective: Director of He Sapa Initiatives Dr. Valeriah Big Eagle, Director of Organizing Eva Cardenas, and Senior Domestic Policy Strategist Davis Price, to learn about their thoughts on voting.

items.title: The tax-subsidized shrug: How foundation leaders threaten democracy and the nonprofit sector
items.summary: A recent report from the Center of Effective Philanthropy may be unable to explain foundation behaviors, it does shine light on the extent of institutional dawdling and misalignment in the nonprofit sector. Why are some foundation executives content with rearranging furniture instead of being active partners in fixing the material realities of a shrinking nonprofit sector and, along with it, the social safety net millions rely on? A recent report from the Center of Effective Philanthropy may be unable to explain foundation behaviors but does shed light on the extent of institutional dawdling and misalignment in the nonprofit sector. CEP’s data reveals a startling disconnect between acknowledging a crisis and actually deploying resources to solve it. What emerges in the latest report is a picture of profound paralysis. Foundation leaders are aware that the sector must evolve but remain locked into a status quo of resource hoarding. According to survey responses from nearly 200 CEOs at the nation’s largest foundations, 98 percent acknowledge that foundations need to change to address society’s needs, yet only 14 percent believe such change is “very likely.” A large majority have chosen not to increase payouts, and the minority that has is moving from a legally mandated 5 percent to 6 or 7 percent at best. Consider the starkest example of the misalignment: Roughly 40 percent of foundation CEOs report offering “support beyond the grant,” yet a statistically negligible 1 percent of nonprofit leaders say non-financial assistance is what their organizations actually need.

items.title: A nonprofit bought a grocery market to fund survivor recovery—can the model deliver?
items.summary: Can a conventional business successfully become part of a nonprofit’s mission infrastructure, generating income while also helping communities? In April 2026, a nonprofit that supports trafficking survivors bought The Pantry, a longstanding grocery market in Fairfield, Connecticut, with plans to run the business as is, using it as a source of earned revenue and a place to create employment opportunities as part of its survivor model. This is not a completely new venture for the organization, Partnership to End Human Trafficking (PEHT). It’s an expansion of existing social enterprise work, since PEHT already operates the PEHT Shop where trafficking survivors are empowered through employment opportunities. The interesting difference between the two ventures is that The Pantry is an established commercial operation with customers, employees, expenses and inventory that come with running a busy grocery business. PEHT’s purchase of The Pantry offers an interesting case study: Can a conventional business successfully become part of a nonprofit’s mission infrastructure, generating income while creating a path to economic independence for survivors? Before PEHT purchased The Pantry, its finances were heavily dependent on charitable donations. Public FY2025 reporting shows that the organization reported $1.95 million in total revenue. Of that, $1.88 million—or about 96 percent—came from grants, contributions, and similar accounts. By comparison, the organization reported new income of $58,619 from fundraising events and $14,959 from sales of inventory.

items.title: Creating Climate Policy That Works Requires Community Data (Blog)
items.summary: Portland residents explained what makes a building livable in a heat wave. Their responses became the basis for statewide climate policy. In June 2021, a heat dome settled over the Pacific Northwest and Portland reached 116 degrees. Nearly 100 Oregonians died of heat-related illness, most of them at home. By then, the Coalition of Communities of Color (CCC) had a long-standing partnership with the City of Portland and was collaborating with community members to design building and energy policy. A community policy workshop took place shortly after the heat dome, bringing residents’ recent experiences of extreme heat directly into the conversation. CCC asked community members what they needed to stay cool and what it was costing them. During these conversations, attendees said the extreme heat wave was stressful. They said it forced impossible choices. Residents said they felt like they were being chased by the mafia. Community members described what they wanted their city to protect, and the values they surfaced became the HEART Standards: Health, Equitable energy, Anti-displacement, Resilience, and Temperature, a community-developed framework for shaping building policy. These standards anchor Portland’s approach to the buildings its residents live in and the climate-resilient policies designed to protect them.

items.title: Money worries cloud voter mobilization efforts
items.summary: With the midterms approaching, nonprofits work to get out the vote. The Voter Participation Center’s massive voter turnout campaign for the midterm elections almost didn’t happen. “The funding did come, but it was late, very late,” said Tom Lopach, the nonprofit’s president. With big plans but not enough money, Lopach and his staff tried in mid-August to decide what to cut. Should it be a digital get-out-the-vote campaign? A massive effort to get people to vote by mail? Or maybe a “social pressure” push that encourages people to join their peers in casting a ballot? But by the end of summer, money came through, and Lopach and his staff were able to roll out a $40 million effort. The center, which consists of both a 501(c)(3) organization and a 501(c)(4), which can devote money to electoral politics, wants to help 500,000 people submit voter registration applications and 400,000 vote-by-mail applications during the current election cycle. Lopach declined to identify which groups and individuals helped the center stay on track, but in the recent past it has received funding from donor-advised funds at Fidelity Charitable and the Silicon Valley Community Foundation as well as the MacArthur Foundation. Nonprofit leaders have made concerted efforts to encourage democracy-related funding over the past two years, perhaps most notably through the All by April campaign, which helped get philanthropy to dedicate $268 million to a range of issues related to voting, combating misinformation and election administration.

items.title: Why direct mail still delivers at year-end in the age of AI
items.summary: Nonprofits large and small are getting more from the mailbox — and in a world of AI-polished copy, a human touch may be their biggest advantage. For many nonprofits, it’s direct mail go-time. The next few weeks will decide whether the year’s fundraising goals are met, and mail still delivers results — even as organizations devote more resources to online channels. The National Park Foundation’s leaders made a major investment in annual giving three years ago, with ambitious goals for increasing digital revenue. Online fundraising indeed grew, but to the organization’s surprise, direct mail grew even more in dollar terms. Its revenue from direct mail jumped from $17.4 million in 2024 to $28.25 million in the fiscal year that ended September 30, accounting for more than half of the nonprofit’s $48.7 million in annual giving. When asked if AI drove that growth curve, Jennifer Harris, its senior vice president for philanthropy, has an immediate answer: No. But smart tools still have a place in designing a better mail campaign, she says. The Chronicle spoke with fundraisers at nonprofits large and small to learn what’s working in the mailbox this season and where technology enhances value. For two decades, the sector asked whether direct mail would survive the shift to digital. Now the question has evolved, says Dan Sonners, director of direct marketing at the watchdog nonprofit Judicial Watch: “Why is direct mail so persistent? Why does it continue to work against the odds?”

items.title: Veteran charities are highly visible but get less than 1 percent of U.S. giving
items.summary: Top 10 recipients captured 85 percent of 2024’s growth to $4 billion, while older membership groups closed. Nonprofits that serve military members and veterans may be a fixture of television and sports sponsorships, but they receive a relatively small share of U.S. charitable giving. And much of their recent growth went to just a few large organizations, according to a new report. Donations to these groups rose 5.9 percent in 2024, to about $4 billion, before adjusting for inflation, data produced by Indiana University’s Lilly Family School of Philanthropy shows. The findings suggest that the growth may say more about the fundraising strength of a few big organizations than about broad donor enthusiasm. The data also doesn’t capture all of the nuances in a field in which some groups may have seen a narrower or no increase in their fundraising totals, experts said. Military and veteran groups’ share of overall U.S. giving was essentially unchanged. It was 0.68 percent in 2024, the most recent year with finalized IRS figures, and has stayed 0.6 to 0.7 percent for a decade.

items.title: Anthropic expands AI support for nonprofits
items.summary: The move comes as Anthropic files to sell shares to the public. Anthropic expanded its support for the nonprofit sector Monday, even as the artificial intelligence company filed to sell shares to the public for the first time. The maker of the AI assistant Claude said the moves are all part of its broader strategy for “compounding good.” Anthropic launched a new Claude for Nonprofits plugin created with 30 nonprofits to be more responsive to their specific needs. It will also broaden its Claude Corps program that embeds fellows with nonprofits to help them better utilize AI by also making consultants available to help organizations with smaller, shorter-term projects. “This work is so core to who we are as a public benefit corporation,” Elizabeth Kelly, Anthropic’s head of beneficial deployments, told The Associated Press. “We were founded to ensure that we’re both developing AI safely and responsibly and that we’re deploying it in a way that really benefits everyone, including those who are too often left behind.” Earlier this month, Anthropic announced plans to commit 5% of its shares to a new Anthropic Public Benefit Fund that could be used for large scale donations to nonprofits or directly distributed to groups of people adversely impacted by AI. The fund still needs to be approved by shareholders once Anthropic completes its IPO, which could come as early as November.

items.title: Stop calling gifts ‘transformational.’ Say what they’ll change.
items.summary: As wealth inequality persists, funders should be as explicit as possible about the impact of their work. Keep up with everything happening in The Commons by signing up for our weekly newsletter. Philanthropy has always lived in an uneasy relationship with inequality. The same concentration of wealth that makes a billion-dollar gift possible can leave people wondering why anyone has a billion dollars to give away in the first place. As extreme wealth has grown, this tension has become harder to ignore. It has contributed to declining trust in philanthropy and left foundations and donors more vulnerable to political attacks over their wealth, influence, and role in public life. Yet philanthropy matters precisely because so many needs go unmet. Markets have little incentive to provide what people cannot afford. And government agencies cannot — or, too often, choose not to — fill every gap. Philanthropy, like it or not, offers a critical boost across many fields: medical research, education, journalism, shelters, community organizing, and more. As government retreats from some of these responsibilities, we may depend even more heavily on the private wealth that people increasingly question.

items.title: How to keep your donors coming back
items.summary: Tips to keep donors loyal to your cause — from easy ways to build a monthly giving program to thanking donors well. Fundraisers pour enormous energy into securing a gift from new donors, only to watch many of those supporters evaporate. The Fundraising Effectiveness Project puts donor retention at just 18 percent as of 2026 — a rate that has barely budged in years. The organizations that break the cycle of loss treat the first gift not as the goal but as the beginning of a relationship they intend to nurture. That mindset reshapes everything from the way a campaign is built to the thank-you note that follows a gift. Instead of concentrating solely on ushering in new donors, these fundraisers design communications around keeping their current donors in the fold. A long-term giving strategy should permeate appeals on every level and in every channel, says Fey Destruti, director of digital strategy at Mercy Ships: “We optimize for the second gift, not the first gift.” These resources will help you keep donors loyal to your cause — from easy ways to build a monthly giving program to holding on to major donors through a leadership change. items.title: Ford’s ‘absolutely seismic’ reboot comes into focus
items.summary: President Heather Gerken's first plan for the grant maker has Ford doubling down on democracy. In her first strategy overhaul as president of the Ford Foundation, Heather Gerken will focus the grant maker squarely on strengthening democracies and ensuring everyone has access to economic opportunity. The emerging strategy is the foundation’s first major reset since its former president, Darren Walker, made equity the grant maker’s focal point in 2014. Since then, Gerken said in an interview, democratic institutions and practices have been demolished or threatened in the United States and globally. “The world has obviously been upended, and we are seeing some of the basic building blocks of democracy undermined here and across the world,” she said. Gerken, who took over as president in January after a tenure as dean of the Yale Law School, is a constitutional law expert who made clear upon her arrival that these issues would take precedence. To make progress in those areas, Ford’s trustees have signed off on Gerken’s plan to reduce the number of program areas from 19 to seven and increase both the number and size of multiyear grants it provides. Ford will also support the broader philanthropic and nonprofit sector with a recently established office of innovation and will create a separate racial justice fund.

items.title: The Ford Foundation will throw more weight behind democracy
items.summary: Seven new programs will be detailed throughout next year. Their impact will reach beyond just issues of democracy. The Ford Foundation, one of the world’s largest private grantmakers, will overhaul its spending to counter what new leadership views as the mutually reinforcing rise of both autocracy and inequality. The New York-based philanthropy committed Thursday to driving more funds toward the basic building blocks of democracy. The new strategic direction comes less than one year into Ford Foundation President Heather Gerken’s tenure at the helm of the social justice funder’s $18 billion endowment. In a report to trustees, Gerken — widely recognized as a leading expert on constitutional law and elections — framed the changes in the context of an “emboldened strain of 21st-century authoritarianism.” Seven new programs — focused on democratic governance, inclusive economies, trustworthy information, public safety, gender equality, global cooperation and racial justice — will be detailed throughout next year. Their impact, Gerken suggested, will reach beyond just issues of democracy. “If you don’t have a rule of law, if you don’t have an election system that functions, all the other values that Ford cares about, all the other projects that Ford has done over the years, fall apart,” she told The Associated Press. “So, protecting marginalized communities, pushing forward on equality, protecting the climate, all of these depend on those basic building blocks.”

items.title: Podcast: Is Philanthropy Fueling Polarization?
items.summary: A conversation with Daniel Stid of the American Enterprise Institute. Has large-scale philanthropic investment in national policy advocacy, over time, deepened American polarization rather than healed it? Daniel Stid, senior fellow at the American Enterprise Institute, believes funders on the left and right have increasingly bankrolled advocates clustered at ideological poles, making it harder for either political party to build governing majorities near the center, where most Americans actually sit. In this podcast interview with Phil Buchanan, president of the Center for Effective Philanthropy, the two also debate whether philanthropically funded efforts to directly oppose the current administration are effective or counterproductive. Stid argues for what he calls “responsible pluralism”: funding advocacy aimed at building durable majorities through Congress, rather than unilateral executive action, regardless of which party wields that power. Buchanan challenges the underlying premise, arguing the current threat to democratic norms and civil society is categorically different from past administrations’ overreach. The two also discuss the nonprofit sector’s dependence on federal funding, a relationship Stid traces back to the Great Society era and what he sees as an unavoidable reckoning now that the decades-long bipartisan consensus supporting that funding relationship has broken down.

items.title: How lean teams can raise more money
items.summary: Resources to help small fundraising teams become mightier through sharper priorities and new tech tools. Small development shops have to do it all with a fraction of the staff found at big nonprofits. They often cultivate donors, plan events, manage donor databases, and write all the appeals — work that larger teams can divide among specialists. It’s understandable to feel that there simply isn’t enough capacity to do it all well. But some of the most effective fundraising happens at organizations with small teams — even one-person shops — that focus their limited energy where it counts, find ways to maximize their time, and avoid spreading themselves thin on projects that aren’t paying off. That last part matters most. A lean team can’t afford to spend time it doesn’t have on appeals that land flat or activities with low return. “Put one foot in front of the other,” advises Holly Moon, assistant director for chapter fundraising at the Sierra Club, where she coaches the leaders of the national environmental group’s 64 local chapters. “It doesn’t have to be perfect. It just has to be heartful and it has to be done.” Here’s a roundup of resources to help small teams become mightier through sharp priorities and new tech tools. items.title: Further Scaling Our Malaria Grantmaking
items.summary: Over the past five years, GiveWell has expanded the scale of our grantmaking and team substantially. We expect to grant more than $1 billion this year, more than double the $418 million we committed in 2025. Alongside this grantmaking growth, we’ve more than doubled the number of researchers on our team since the start of last year. A larger team means we can investigate a greater number of both more complex and larger funding opportunities than we could before. One area where we expect our grantmaking to increase substantially in the coming years is the prevention and treatment of malaria. From 2027 through 2032, we’re aiming to grant at least $2.5 billion in new malaria funding, potentially several times that amount. The total amount will depend on the funding we have available, the feasibility of scaling up cost-effective malaria programs, countries’ appetite for those programs, and how opportunities within malaria compare to other grantmaking areas. This expanded support could go to organizations we currently fund (such as the Against Malaria Foundation and Malaria Consortium), as well as to new organizations and novel funding vehicles.
